The Story of Shripanik Muni

I bow to Lord Jinendra, the bestower of happiness and worshipped by the noble, and I write the story of Shripanik Muni, which brings welfare to all.

In the city of Panishwar, during the reign of King Prajapal, there lived a merchant named Sagardatt. His wife was Panika. They had a son named Panik. Panik was simple, peaceful, and pure-hearted. Sin never touched him. He always walked the path of righteousness.

One day, he went to the Lord's Samavasaran, which was adorned with jewelled arches of great beauty and whose majestic pillars delighted all who beheld it. There he saw Lord Vardhaman seated on the Gandhakuti. The Lord's splendour at that time was extraordinary and worthy of being seen. He was seated on a jewelled golden throne. Three canopies, surpassing the full moon in brilliance, shone above him. Bright as pearl necklaces, divine chowries waved over him. The radiance of his body outshone the combined light of many suns. He was teaching through a divine voice that dispelled all manner of doubts. The sky and earth resounded with the drums of the gods. Indra, Dharanendra, Chakravartins, Vidyadharas, and great kings came and worshipped him. Many Nirgrantha monks praised him and felt fulfilled. Adorned with thirty-four types of superlative attributes, he possessed the four infinites — infinite vision, infinite knowledge, infinite bliss, and infinite energy. He was honoured as the supreme being of the universe. Seeing and knowing all three worlds clearly, he taught the worthy souls their true nature. For him, the beautiful maiden of liberation stood ready with a garland in her hand.

Seeing the Lord's divine form, Panik bowed his head, worshipped and praised him, circumambulated him, and sat to hear the discourse. In the end, he realised that his lifespan was very short. In such a state, attending to the soul's welfare was most urgent. So Panik took initiation right there and became a monk.

From there, wandering and teaching dharma in many lands and cities, Monk Panik one day came to the banks of the Ganga. To cross the river, he boarded a boat. As the boatman was rowing, suddenly a storm arose as if the end of the world had come. The boat began to sink. All the passengers were terrified. But Panik Muni remained calm. He sat in meditation, unshaken by the danger. The boat sank, and all those who were attached to their bodies perished. But Panik, through the power of his meditation and the purity of his conduct, was carried safely to the other shore by the current. He continued his spiritual practice and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that those who are pure in heart and devoted to dharma are protected even in the greatest dangers. Panik's calmness in the face of death saved him, while those who were attached to their bodies and panicked perished. The wise should cultivate inner peace and detachment, for these are the true safeguards in the storms of life.
